body_en:
It's hard to imagine what you've never seen, so people picture South Korea's chaebols through their own assumptions.

Many Chinese people, picturing South Korea, automatically conjure the same image: the heads of Samsung, Hyundai, and SK sitting around a table deciding the country's affairs, the president reduced to a hired manager carrying out their will, lawmakers and officials orbiting the chaebols.

Hence the claims all over the internet: Samsung accounts for a huge share of Korea's economy, the Korean president is just a chaebol employee, South Korea is really a “chaebol republic.”

The chaebols do wield astonishing economic power and social influence. But follow that logic one step further, and you run into a problem that's hard to explain.

If the chaebols really controlled Korean politics, what is the one thing Korea should least have?

Most people would think of the opposition, the media, or social movements. But for capital, the thing that can directly threaten corporate profits and business order has never been public opinion — it's unions.

If the chaebols truly held overwhelming political power, the first thing they should have done is wipe out unions entirely.

Yet reality is the opposite. South Korea doesn't just have unions — it has some of the strongest, best-organized unions in Asia.

To understand that, you have to start with one man: Han Sang-gyun.

Now in his sixties, Han no longer charges at the front lines the way he did in his youth, but he still carries enormous influence in Korea's labor movement.

He once led the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, the country's largest labor federation, organizing strikes and labor actions for years — and served prison time for it.

In the eyes of many Korean workers, his authority doesn't come from slogans. It comes from having been in the fiercest labor conflicts himself.

When Ssangyong Motor carried out mass layoffs in 2009, the union and management clashed violently. Workers occupied the factory for weeks, locked in a standoff with police. The government sent in large numbers of riot police; helicopters, tear gas, and force were deployed in turn, and the plant at one point resembled a battlefield.

Whatever you think of that conflict, it proves one thing: even against the government and a major corporation, Korean unions still have formidable organizing and mobilizing power.

Many people see this and think Korean society is too chaotic. But look at it from another angle, and a more interesting question emerges.

If the chaebols really controlled Korean politics, why would they allow this to happen? Why not simply have the government break up the unions? Why not eliminate these organizations once and for all? Why did it still end at the negotiating table?

The reason is simple. Powerful as the chaebols are, they are not powerful enough to dominate the whole of society.

Samsung is the clearest example.

As Korea's most powerful conglomerate, Samsung has long been seen as the face of the chaebol system.

It employs hundreds of thousands of people, dominates Korea's most important industry — semiconductors — and carries enormous weight in exports, employment, and tax revenue. By almost any measure, Samsung is one of the most important engines of the Korean economy.

And yet this company spent decades fighting unions, and still ended up having to accept them.

Samsung's founder, Lee Byung-chul, held to a no-union philosophy throughout his life. For a long time, Samsung was considered one of the hardest companies in Korea in which to organize a union.

Many Korean labor activists regarded getting a union into Samsung as a nearly impossible task. But in 2020, Samsung formally abandoned its no-union tradition.

In the years that followed, the Samsung Electronics union grew rapidly, reaching tens of thousands of members and becoming one of the largest enterprise unions in Korea.

Even more symbolic: in 2024, Samsung saw its first large-scale general strike in more than fifty years. And the strikers were no longer just assembly-line workers — they were chip engineers, researchers, and technical staff.

These are people who hold key links in the world's most advanced semiconductor production chain. When they stop work, the company's losses are measured by the hour.

So people witnessed a striking reversal. The Samsung that had once flatly opposed unions began negotiating with them proactively; management started discussing bonuses, profit-sharing, and employee benefits.

And the Korean government, worried about the impact on the semiconductor industry, kept stepping in to mediate, urging both sides to compromise.

The most striking thing here is this: the union wasn't begging Samsung to negotiate. It was the other way around — Samsung had to take the union's demands seriously. Even the Korean government couldn't simply order the union to end its action; it could only play coordinator and mediator.

And that reveals something many people overlook.

Power doesn't come in only one form: capital.

Wealth is a form of power. Administrative power is a form of power. Judicial power is a form of power. Media influence is a form of power. And the ability to organize tens of thousands — hundreds of thousands — of people to stop work at the same time is also a form of power.

One engineer quitting means nothing to Samsung. But thousands of engineers stopping work at once is a different matter entirely. One worker marching in the street may not concern the government. But hundreds of thousands acting together is something no government can ignore.

The most important function of a union is to take scattered individuals and organize them into a collective force capable of negotiating with capital and government.

The chaebols are strong, but the unions are strong too. The government holds administrative power, but it also has to answer to votes and social pressure. The sides cooperate and check each other; no one can completely dominate the rest. South Korea has built a system of democratic checks and balances.

A chaebol group that can't even fully control its own workers — how could it control an entire country?
excerpt_en: Everyone “knows” Samsung and Hyundai run South Korea. But there's one thing a chaebol-controlled country should never have — and South Korea has some of Asia's strongest unions. That contradiction tells the real story.
title_en: The Truth About South Korea's Chaebols and Politics
